categories.name: Bamboo
categories.description: The grove, the cut and the seasons.

categories.name: Living with baskets
categories.description: Use, care and repair at home.

posts.title: Why we cut bamboo in winter
posts.excerpt: In the cold weeks the culms rest and the sap sinks. That is when bamboo stays pale, light and safe from insects.
posts.content:
We wait for the first hard frost, then walk the grove with a saw and a pot of chalk. Only three-year culms get a mark: younger ones bend too much, older ones turn brittle.

A cut culm leans against the others for a week before we carry it down, so it dries slowly from the inside and does not split.

posts.title: Splitting a culm into twenty-four strips
posts.excerpt: One knife, one block of wood and a steady hand. Here is how a single culm becomes the strips for a bread basket.
posts.content:
The knife goes in at the top and the culm opens by itself along the grain. We split in halves, then quarters, and keep halving until each piece is as wide as a finger.

Then the soft inner layer is peeled away, and the strips hang in the loft until they are needed.

posts.title: Caring for a bamboo basket
posts.excerpt: Water is not the enemy: a quick rinse, a dry corner in the shade and a basket lasts for decades.
posts.content:
Rinse a basket under the tap and brush out the crumbs with a soft brush. Shake it, then let it dry in an airy spot out of direct sun.

Over the years the pale bamboo turns honey brown. That colour is the basket getting stronger, not older.
